title: Lead, kindly light (Newman, 1833)
hookLine: written at sea, becalmed: one step enough for me
tomorrow: why would a poet compare God's glory to shaken foil?

cards: Night driving on a back road. The headlights reach the next stretch, and past that it's black. Nobody sees the whole drive home that way, and still the car gets home.

John Henry Newman, yesterday's writer, was on a ship becalmed at sea, no wind, far from home, when he wrote a poem asking for exactly that much light and no more: "I do not ask to see The distant scene; one step enough for me."

teach.h: LEAD: HE DOESN'T ASK FOR THE MAP.
teach.b: First, the request. The night is dark, he's far from home, and he asks to be led. He doesn't ask for the map.

teach.h: I LOVED TO CHOOSE AND SEE MY PATH.
teach.b: Second, the confession, and it's what makes that first stanza land: "I loved to choose and see my path; but now Lead Thou me on!" He used to want the whole map, with his own hand on it.
Pride ruled his will, he says, and he asks God not to remember past years. So one step enough isn't a calm personality talking. It's a change of heart.
He looks back on how long he's been blessed, and trusts the same power to lead him on, "O'er moor and fen, o'er crag and torrent, till The night is gone".
Bog, cliff and flood, one step at a time, and not one of them skipped.
Fourth, the morning: "And with the morn those angel faces smile, Which I have loved long since, and lost awhile."
Who are those faces? The poem doesn't say, and some readers still wonder.
One to tell a friend: Newman's own title for it was The Pillar of the Cloud, after the cloud that went before Israel in the desert by day, showing the way.

how: Newman's poem is sung as the hymn Lead, Kindly Light by Catholics and Anglicans, and some people pray it at turning points when the road ahead can't be seen.

o: a request to be guided, one step at a time
an order to take charge and go first
a gray metal once used in church windows

games.q: the poem from the ship — tap the pairs.
p: I loved to choose and see my path
the road, crossed step by step
angel faces, loved and lost awhile

s: Newman wrote this because he was naturally calm about the future
the second stanza confesses he loved to choose and see his path.
Newman asks to see the distant scene
he asks the opposite: one step enough for me.
the poem ends in morning light
and with the morn those angel faces smile.

games.q: your aunt just lost her job and is up at 2 a.m. building a budget for next year. which line of Newman's poem fits her night?
o: I loved to choose and see my path.
o'er moor and fen, o'er crag and torrent.
games.why: the first stanza asks for no more light than the next step. 'I loved to choose and see my path' is the old habit he's confessing, not the prayer.

practice: Stand and take a few slow steps across the room, or simply feel your feet press the floor where you are. Let each step carry the line: one step enough for me. If you pray, you can add Newman's words, lead thou me on.

wordCard.voice: Lead. Newman's one-word request in the dark: not show me everything, just lead. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one step enough. He loved to see the whole path, then asked only for the next step. Rest well.
